tip: A SIP doesn't need a 'perfect' market entry point by design — that's the entire reason it exists. Trying to also time when you start your SIP defeats its purpose.
Comparing a fund's 1-year return against a 10-year return tells you more about recent market conditions than about the fund's actual skill — always check returns across multiple timeframes.

A flexi-cap fund can invest across large, mid, and small-cap stocks freely, giving the fund manager more flexibility — and more responsibility for getting the allocation right — than a fund locked into one market-cap category.
Two funds in the same category can have very different risk levels depending on how concentrated their top 10 holdings are — check portfolio concentration, not just the category label.
A fund's 'AUM' (Assets Under Management) size can affect strategy flexibility — a very large small-cap fund, for instance, may struggle to deploy new money into genuinely small, less liquid stocks.
Step-up SIPs let you automatically increase your monthly SIP amount by a fixed percentage every year, matching rising income without needing a manual decision each time.

A multi-cap fund is required to maintain minimum allocations across large, mid, and small-cap stocks by regulation, while a flexi-cap fund has no such mandated minimums — read the mandate, not just the name.
If you hold 5 'different' large-cap funds, check their portfolios — large-cap funds often hold many of the same top stocks, meaning your 'diversification' may be smaller than it looks on paper.

A fund's benchmark matters: a mid-cap fund should be judged against a mid-cap index, not against the Nifty 50 — comparing against the wrong benchmark can make a fund look better or worse than it really is.
SIP in index funds removes manager selection risk entirely — you're not betting on whether a specific fund manager will outperform, only on the broader market's long-term growth.

Hybrid/balanced advantage funds automatically shift the equity-debt mix based on market valuation signals, aiming to reduce the emotional burden of manual rebalancing — useful for investors who don't want to actively manage allocation.
A sudden change in a fund's manager is worth noting — historical performance was generated under the old manager's decisions, and a new manager may run the fund differently going forward.

SIP 'pause' facilities let you skip a few months without formally stopping the mandate — useful during temporary cash flow stress, without losing your SIP registration and having to restart from scratch.

A thematic fund (e.g., 'infrastructure,' 'manufacturing') concentrates risk in one theme — it can outperform sharply when that theme is in favor, and underperform sharply when it isn't. Size the allocation accordingly.

Fund factsheets publish the portfolio turnover ratio — a high turnover ratio often means more frequent buying/selling, which can mean higher transaction costs and potentially higher short-term tax impact within the fund.

An international/global fund adds genuine geographic diversification beyond the Indian market, but also adds currency risk — rupee depreciation can boost returns, and rupee appreciation can dampen them, independent of the underlying market's performance.

Target maturity debt funds hold bonds until a specific maturity date, giving relatively predictable, bond-like returns if held to that date — useful for goal-based debt allocation with a known time horizon.

A fund's 'standard deviation' and 'Sharpe ratio,' both published in factsheets, give a quick sense of how volatile a fund has been and how well it has been compensated for that volatility — worth checking alongside raw returns.
Switching funds frequently chasing recent outperformance (called 'return chasing') is one of the most studied, most common ways retail investors underperform the very funds they invest in.
A SIP's XIRR (not simple average return) is the correct way to measure your actual annualized return, since it accounts for the different dates and amounts of each individual instalment.
